{{Short description|Variation of a finite automaton that runs on infinite input}}
{{Lowercase title}}

In [[automata theory]], a branch of [[theoretical computer science]], an '''[[Ordinal number|ω]]-automaton''' (or '''stream automaton''') is a variation of a [[finite automaton]] that runs on infinite, rather than finite, strings as input. Since ω-automata do not stop, they have a variety of acceptance conditions rather than simply a set of accepting states.

ω-automata are useful for specifying behavior of systems that are not expected to terminate, such as hardware, [[operating systems]] and [[control systems]]. For such systems, one may want to specify a property such as "for every request, an acknowledge eventually follows", or its negation "there is a request that is not followed by an acknowledge". The former is a property of infinite words: one cannot say of a finite sequence that it satisfies this property.

Classes of ω-automata include the [[Büchi automaton|Büchi automata]], Rabin automata, Streett automata, parity automata and [[Muller automaton|Muller automata]], each deterministic or non-deterministic. These classes of ω-automata differ only in terms of [[ω-automaton#Acceptance conditions|acceptance condition]]. They all recognize precisely the [[omega-regular language|regular ω-language]]s except for the deterministic Büchi automata, which is strictly weaker than all the others. Although all these types of automata recognize the same set of [[ω-language]]s, they nonetheless differ in succinctness of representation for a given ω-language.

==Deterministic ω-automata==
Formally, a '''deterministic ω-automaton''' is a [[tuple]] {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A = (Q,\Sigma,\delta,Q_0,A_{acc})</math>,}} that consists of the following components:
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q</math>,}} is a [[finite set]]. The elements of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q</math>}} are called the ''states'' of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}}.
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Sigma</math>,}} is a finite set called the ''alphabet'' of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}}.
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \delta \colon Q \times \Sigma \rightarrow Q</math>}} is a function, called the ''transition function'' of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}}.
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q_0</math>}} is an element of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q</math>}}, called the initial state.
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A_{acc}</math>}} is a set of ''accepting'' states of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}}, formally a subset of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q^\omega</math>}}.
An ''input'' for {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} is an infinite string over the alphabet {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Sigma</math>}}, i.e. it is an infinite sequence {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \alpha = (a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots)</math>}}.
The ''run'' of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} on such an input is an infinite sequence {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \rho = (r_0, r_1, r_2, \ldots)</math>}} of states, defined as follows:

* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r_0 = q_0</math>}}.
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r_1 = \delta(r_0, a_1)</math>}}.
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r_2 = \delta(r_1, a_2)</math>}}.
:: ...
* that is, for every {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> i</math>}}: {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r_i = \delta(r_{i-1}, a_i)</math>}}.

The main purpose of an ω-automaton is to define a subset of the set of all inputs: The set of ''accepted'' inputs. Whereas in the case of an ordinary finite automaton every run ends with a state {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r_n</math>}} and the input is accepted if and only if {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r_n</math>}} is an accepting state, the definition of the set of accepted inputs is more complicated for ω-automata. Here we must look at the entire run {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \rho</math>}}. The input is accepted if the corresponding run is in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \text{Acc}</math>}}. The set of accepted input ω-words is called the ''recognized ω-language'' by the automaton, which is denoted as {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L(A)</math>}}.

The definition of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \text{Acc}</math>}} as a subset of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q^\omega</math>}} is purely formal and not suitable for practice because normally such sets are infinite. The difference between various types of ω-automata (Büchi, Rabin etc.) consists in how they encode certain subsets {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \text{Acc}</math>}} of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q^\omega</math>}} as finite sets, and therefore in which such subsets they can encode.

==Nondeterministic ω-automata==
Formally, a '''nondeterministic ω-automaton''' is a tuple {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A = (Q, \Sigma, \Delta, Q_0, \text{Acc})</math>}} that consists of the following components:
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q</math>}} is a [[finite set]]. The elements of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q</math>}} are called the ''states'' of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}}.
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Sigma</math>}} is a finite set called the ''alphabet'' of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}}.
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta</math>}} is a subset of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q \times \Sigma \times Q</math>}} and is called the ''transition relation'' of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}}.
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q_0</math>}} is a subset of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q</math>}}, called the initial set of states.
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \text{Acc}</math>}} is the ''acceptance condition'', a subset of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q^\omega</math>}}.
Unlike a deterministic ω-automaton, which has a transition function {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \delta</math>}}, the non-deterministic version has a transition relation {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta</math>}}. Note that {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta</math>}} can be regarded as a function {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q \times \Sigma \rightarrow \mathcal{P}(Q)</math>}} from {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q \times \Sigma</math>}} to the [[power set]] {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \mathcal{P}(Q)</math>}}. Thus, given a state {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> q_n</math>}} and a symbol {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> a_n</math>}}, the next state {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> q_{n+1}</math>}} is not necessarily determined uniquely, rather there is a set of possible next states.

A ''run'' of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} on the input {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \alpha = (a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots)</math>}} is any infinite sequence {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \rho = (r_0, r_1, r_2, \ldots)</math>}} of states that satisfies the following conditions:
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r_0</math>}} is an element of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q_0</math>}}.
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r_1</math>}} is an element of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta(r_0, a_1)</math>}}.
* {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r_2</math>}} is an element of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta(r_1, a_2)</math>}}.
:: ...
* that is, for every {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> i</math>}}: {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> r_i</math>}} is an element of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta(r_{i-1}, a_i)</math>}}.

A nondeterministic ω-automaton may admit many different runs on any given input, or none at all. The input is accepted if at least one of the possible runs is accepting. Whether a run is accepting depends only on {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \text{Acc}</math>}}, as for deterministic ω-automata.
Every deterministic ω-automaton can be regarded as a nondeterministic ω-automaton by taking {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta</math>}} to be the graph of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \delta</math>}}. The definitions of runs and acceptance for deterministic ω-automata are then special cases of the nondeterministic cases.

==Acceptance conditions==

Acceptance conditions may be infinite sets of ω-words. However, people mostly study acceptance conditions that are finitely representable. The following lists a variety of popular acceptance conditions.

Before discussing the list, let's make the following observation. In the case of infinitely running systems, one is often interested in whether certain behavior is repeated infinitely often. For example, if a network card receives infinitely many ping requests, then it may fail to respond to some of the requests but should respond to an infinite subset of received ping requests. This motivates the following definition: For any run {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \rho</math>}}, let {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \text{Inf}(\rho)</math>}} be the set of states that occur infinitely often in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \rho</math>}}. This notion of certain states being visited infinitely often will be helpful in defining the following acceptance conditions.

*A [[Büchi automaton]] is an ω-automaton {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} that uses the following acceptance condition, for some subset {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> F</math>}} of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q</math>}}:
:;Büchi condition: {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} accepts exactly those runs {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \rho</math>}} for which {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \text{Inf}(\rho) \cap F \neq \emptyset</math>}}, i.e. there is an accepting state that occurs infinitely often in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \rho</math>}}.

*A '''{{vanchor|Rabin automaton}}''' is an ω-automaton {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} that uses the following acceptance condition, for some set {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Omega</math>}} of pairs {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> (B_i, G_i)</math>}} of sets of states:

:;Rabin condition: {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} accepts exactly those runs {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \rho</math>}} for which there exists a pair {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> (B_i, G_i)</math>}} in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Omega</math>}} such that {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> B_i \cap \text{Inf}(\rho) = \emptyset</math>}} and {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> G_i \cap \text{Inf}(\rho) \neq \emptyset</math>}}.

*A '''Streett automaton''' is an ω-automaton {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} that uses the following acceptance condition, for some set {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Omega</math>}} of pairs {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> (B_i, G_i)</math>}} of sets of states:

:;Streett condition: {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} accepts exactly those runs {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \rho</math>}} such that for all pairs {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> (B_i, G_i)</math>}} in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Omega</math>}}, {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> B_i \cap \text{Inf}(\rho) \neq \emptyset</math>}} or {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> G_i \cap \text{Inf}(\rho) = \emptyset</math>}}.

*A '''parity automaton''' is an automaton {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} whose set of states is {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, k\}</math>}} for some natural number {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> k</math>}}, and that has the following acceptance condition:
:;Parity condition: {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} accepts {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \rho</math>}} [[if and only if]] the smallest number in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \text{Inf}(\rho)</math>}} is even.

*A [[Muller automaton]] is an ω-automaton {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} that uses the following acceptance condition, for a subset {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \mathbf{F}</math>}} of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \mathcal{P}(Q)</math>}} (the [[power set]] of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q</math>}}):
:;Muller condition: {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} accepts exactly those runs {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \rho</math>}} for which {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \text{Inf}(\rho) \in \mathbf{F}</math>}}.

Every Büchi automaton can be regarded as a Muller automaton. It suffices to replace {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> F</math>}} by {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \mathbf{F}'</math>}} consisting of all subsets of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> Q</math>}} that contain at least one element of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> F</math>}}.
Similarly every Rabin, Streett or parity automaton can also be regarded as a Muller automaton.

==Example==
[[Image:Buchi non deterministic example.svg|thumb|175px|A non-deterministic Büchi automaton that recognizes (0∪1)*0<sup>ω</sup>]]
The following ω-language {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L</math>}} over the alphabet {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Sigma = \{0, 1\}</math>}}, which can be recognized by a nondeterministic Büchi automaton:
{{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L</math>}} consists of all ω-words in {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Sigma^\omega</math>}} in which 1 occurs only finitely many times.
A non-deterministic Büchi automaton recognizing {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> L</math>}} needs only two states {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> q_0</math>}} (the initial state) and {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> q_1</math>}}. {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Delta</math>}} consists of the triples {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> (q_0, 0, q_0)</math>}}, {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> (q_0, 1, q_0)</math>}}, {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> (q_0, 0, q_1)</math>}} and {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> (q_1, 0, q_1)</math>}}.
{{nowrap|<math display="inline"> F = \{q_1\}</math>}}. For any input {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \alpha</math>}} in which 1 occurs only finitely many times, there is a run that stays in state {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> q_0</math>}} as long as there are 1s to read, and goes to state {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> q_1</math>}} afterwards. This run is successful.
If there are infinitely many 1s, then there is only one possible run: the one that always stays in state {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> q_0</math>}}. (Once the machine has left {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> q_0</math>}} and reached {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> q_1</math>}}, it cannot return. If another 1 is read, there is no successor state.)

Notice that above language cannot be recognized by a deterministic [[Büchi automaton]], which is [[Büchi_automaton#Recognizable_languages|strictly less expressive]] than its non-deterministic counterpart.

==Expressive power of ω-automata==
An ω-language over a finite alphabet {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Sigma</math>}} is a set of ω-words over {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Sigma</math>}}, i.e. it is a subset of {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Sigma^\omega</math>}}. An ω-language over {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> \Sigma</math>}} is said to be recognized by an ω-automaton {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}} (with the same alphabet) if it is the set of all ω-words accepted by {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> A</math>}}.
The expressive power of a class of ω-automata is measured by the class of all ω-languages that can be recognized by some automaton in the class.

The nondeterministic Büchi, parity, Rabin, Streett, and Muller automata, respectively, all recognize exactly the same class of ω-languages.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Safra | first = S. | authorlink = Shmuel Safra
 | contribution = On the complexity of ω-automata
 | doi = 10.1109/SFCS.1988.21948
 | location = Washington, DC, USA
 | pages = 319–327
 | publisher = IEEE Computer Society
 | title = Proceedings of the 29th Annual [[Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science]] (FOCS '88)
 | year = 1988}}.</ref>
These are known as the ''ω-Kleene closure of the regular languages'' or as the [[omega-regular language|regular ω-languages]].
Using different proofs it can also be shown that the deterministic parity, Rabin, Streett, and Muller automata all recognize the regular ω-languages.
It follows from this that the class of regular ω-languages is closed under complementation.
However, the example above shows that the class of deterministic Büchi automata is strictly weaker.

==Conversion between ω-automata==

Because nondeterministic Muller, Rabin, Streett, parity, and Büchi automata are equally expressive, they can be translated to each other.
Let us use the following abbreviation <math>\{N,D\}\times\{M,R,S,P,B\}</math>: for example, ''NB'' stands for nondeterministic Büchi ω-automaton, while ''DP'' stands for deterministic parity ω-automaton. Then the following holds.
* Clearly, any [[deterministic automaton]] can be viewed as a nondeterministic one.
* <math>NB \rightarrow NR/NS/NP</math> with no blow-up in the state space.
* <math>NR \rightarrow NB</math> with a polynomial blow-up in the state space, i.e., the number of states in the resulting ''NB'' is <math>2nm+1</math>, where <math>n</math> is the number of states in the ''NB'' and <math>m</math> is the number of Rabin acceptance pairs (see, for example,<ref>{{citation | last=Esparza | first=Javier | title=Automata Theory: An Algorithmic Approach|url=https://www7.in.tum.de/~esparza/autoskript.pdf|date=2017}}</ref>).
* <math>NS/NM/NP \rightarrow NB</math> with exponential blow-up in the state space.
* <math>NB \rightarrow DR/DP</math> with exponential blow-up in the state space. This determinization result uses [[Safra's construction]].
A comprehensive overview of translations can be found on the referenced web source.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.faculty.idc.ac.il/udiboker/automata/wat.html
 |title=Word-Automata Translations
 |last=Boker |first=Udi |date=18 April 2018 |website=Udi Boker's webpage |access-date=30 March 2019}}</ref>

==Applications to decidability==

ω-automata can be used to prove decidability of S1S, the [[monadic second-order logic | monadic second-order]] (MSO) theory of natural numbers under successor.  [[infinite-tree automaton | Infinite-tree automata]] extend ω-automata to infinite trees and can be used to prove decidability of [[S2S (mathematics) | S2S]], the MSO theory with two successors, and this can be extended to the MSO theory of graphs with bounded (given a fixed bound) [[treewidth]].
